what_the_paper_would_let_us_do: Implement irbesartan from a source with first-order absorption. The only model read in full, Karatza and Karalis 2020 (PMID 32736091, in the archive; two compartments, apparent oral, 32 healthy men, no covariates), absorbs each dose through a delay differential equation, dA0/dt = -ka A0(t - T), with ka T = 0.511 > 1/e, so its input oscillates: 105% of the dose reaches plasma by 6.5 h and 5% flows back to the gut. No nonnegative input the engine can carry gets within 3.5% of that curve (a linear program over any number of pulses), and the best pulse discretisation built (12 default-form oral pulses, as hydrochlorothiazide's Weibull) misses it by 5.8% of the peak (6.4% at a 45 kg woman), ten times the 0.53% standard of docs/adding-a-drug.md, so irbesartan was withheld from PR #818. [decision] for Steven Shafer, raised 2026-11-19: accept Karatza with the 5.8% error stated, or wait for Hedaya and Helmy 2015 (PMID 25545238), whose model the Karatza paper borrowed for its blood-pressure simulations and which is expected to be first order (to be confirmed on the PDF). Karatza's model checked against the Avapro label (not fitted to it): CL/F 13.5 L/h inside the label's 11.8-17.6; Tmax 1.9 h inside 1.5-2 h; terminal half-life 8.2 h against 11-15 h. Karatza's text says nothing is absorbed for the first 1.68 h, but its Table 3 (Tmax 1-2 h at delays to 2.3 h) needs the dose held in the depot before time 0 (Monolix's history convention); that reading reproduces Table 3's Tmax exactly and AUC(0-48) within 0.8%. The Karatza draft (model, test, shared-file patch with the antihypertensive registry record and parameter rows) was not committed; its help-page narrative must be rewritten. Also needed whichever source is used: the drugDefaults row (Antihypertensives), a therapeuticRanges row (none_established), the pregnancy row (not_applicable, ARB fetotoxicity, as valsartan), the antihypertensive registry record and parameters, the three plasma-only rosters, and the Avapro label (archive copy NJ_dailymed-7885b2a8.pdf, md5 12123dca3f7ee8305bd81501a8cc7b64, card papers/digests/NJ_dailymed-7885b2a8.md) in papers/labels with its fdaLabels.csv row.

Liu M, Hu X, Liu J. The effect of hypothermia on isoflurane MAC in children. Anesthesiology 2001;94:429-432. The code says it was read, but its PDF is not in stanpumpRPapers (the archive check in docs/gas-engine-audit/PROMPT.md, section 9), so nobody can re-check the numbers against the source. File the PDF, write its card, and confirm each number below on the PDF. If one differs, change the constant and everything that pins or prints it, in a new pull request. The volatile agents' MAC rests on this paper's regression of isoflurane MAC on temperature in children (37, 34 and 31 C): MAC = 0.0784 T - 1.203. That gives GAS_MAC_ZERO_TEMPERATURE = 1.203/0.0784 = 15.3 C, or 4.6% of the normothermic MAC per degree. The R/physiology.R header says the paper's own text gives 'approximately 5.1%' and a zero at 16.2 C, neither of which follows from its regression. Check all three on the PDF. gasMacTemperatureFactor() applies the regression to sevoflurane, isoflurane and desflurane, to their MAC equivalents, and, since PR #858, to their thresholds (gasThresholdForTemperature()). A copy, PMID_11374601.pdf, is on Dr Shafer's Drive outside the archive, in the folders named CarlisleDownload.

Check the borrowed disposition against the one human measurement there is. R/drugs_carfentanil.R uses sufentanil's disposition on Shafer's judgement, its header saying no human carfentanil kinetics exist and that every human study is PET radiotracer work. Uddayasankar 2018 (Pharmacotherapy 38:e41-e45, doi 10.1002/phar.2117) contradicts that: a recreational exposure with three timed blood samples modelled, an elimination half-life of 5.7 h for carfentanil and 11.8 h for norcarfentanil, and awakening with spontaneous breathing at an interpolated blood concentration of 0.52 ng/mL. Sufentanil's terminal half-life is about 2.5-3.5 h, so that figure points to carfentanil being SLOWER than the congener the model borrows from, the direction the help page already warns about. Read the three sample times and concentrations, the assay, and how the half-life was fitted; then correct the header's and the card's claims either way, and decide (Shafer) whether one case at three samples can move the model's basis or only its documentation. The narrower claim, that no published human population MODEL exists, survives this paper.

what_the_paper_would_let_us_do: Refute the model header's claim that the only in-vivo carfentanil kinetics are in rats, and see whether a second species supports the borrowed disposition's shape. Mutlow 2004 (J Zoo Wildl Med 35:489-96, doi 10.1638/03-074) gives carfentanil pharmacokinetics in eight domestic goats, serial blood to 120 h by LC-MS, rapid absorption and a biphasic decline over 12-48 h. IMPORTANT, and the reason this row was rewritten on 2026-11-25 (CodeRabbit on PR #888): the route is INTRAMUSCULAR only. Every goat had carfentanil 40 ug/kg i.m.; the intravenous, intramuscular and subcutaneous crossover named in the abstract's first sentence is NALTREXONE's, the reversal drug. So this paper gives no intravenous carfentanil arm and no absolute volume or clearance, exactly as Bergh 2019 does not -- the row first claimed the opposite, from reading that sentence and not the rest of the abstract. Read the biphasic parameters and the goats' weights; treat them as evidence about the molecule's shape in a second species, never as a parameter source for people. No intravenous carfentanil study appears in the peer-reviewed literature, but do not write that as an absolute: CodeRabbit pointed at a Feasel 2017 dissertation and a 2018 technical report said to dose four rabbits intravenously, neither of which could be opened (HTTP 403). PubMed's four Feasel carfentanil papers are in vitro or an inhalation biomarker study, so the grey literature is the only open question -- and a dissertation with an intravenous arm would be the first absolute carfentanil disposition in any species. Check it before stating anything absolute in the model header.

what_the_paper_would_let_us_do: A third species' carfentanil kinetics, and the only large-mammal half-life beside the goat's. Cole 2006 (J Zoo Wildl Med 37:318-26, doi 10.1638/05-070.1) gave carfentanil 0.0169 mg/kg intramuscularly to six female common eland with xylazine, sampled the jugular serially to 48 h by LC-MS, and reports Cmax at 13.8 min and a half-life of 7.7 h. Read the clearance, volume and the shape of the decline. Why it matters: carfentanil's model borrows sufentanil's disposition (terminal half-life about 2.5-3.5 h), and the three in-vivo half-lives now known run 35-64 min in the rat, 7.7 h in the eland and 5.7 h in the one human case report -- so both large mammals measured look SLOWER than the congener borrowed from. Intramuscular, so no absolute volume or clearance, and an eland is not a person; this is evidence about the molecule's elimination, never a parameter source. Found by CodeRabbit on PR #888 after this card had twice over-claimed that no second species existed.

Ihmsen H, Geisslinger G, Schuttler J. Stereoselective pharmacokinetics of ketamine: R(-)-ketamine inhibits the elimination of S(+)-ketamine. Clin Pharmacol Ther 2001;70(5):431-438. Steven L. Shafer asked (2026-11-25) whether the library's ketamine (racemate, Domino 1984) describes esketamine. Its abstract reports a crossover in the same 10 volunteers, arterial samples, 2- and 3-compartment fits: S(+)-ketamine clearance 26.3 mL/kg/min given alone, against 14.8 for racemic ketamine and 18.5 for S(+) within the racemate. Perez-Ruixo 2021's IV esketamine clearance (109-114 L/h, about 24.5 mL/kg/min at its 74-kg median) agrees. Read on the PDF: (1) its S(+)-ketamine three-compartment parameters, which could become R/drugs_esketamine.R directly (intravenous, arterial, volunteers), and (2) its racemic parameters against R/drugs_ketamine.R's 13.2 mL/kg/min. Either implement esketamine from it, or apply its within-subject clearance ratio to the library's ketamine; the choice is the [decision] on papers/digests/PMID_33128208.md. A time to peak effect still needs Sigtermans 2009 (PMID 19741495).

Peyton PJ, Robinson GJ, Thompson B. Ventilation-perfusion inhomogeneity increases gas uptake: theoretical modeling of gas exchange. J Appl Physiol 2001;91:3-9. The two-compartment model of the trio: the place to check the mathematics most directly. Filed in the archive (Paper management session, 2026-11-25), not yet carded. stanpumpR's gas engine has one well-mixed lung with ventilation and perfusion matched, so arterial tension equals alveolar. Shafer DECIDED (2026-11-25) to keep the single mixed lung for now: he accepts Peyton's measurements ('data are data') but has concerns about Peyton's mathematics of uptake and distribution. So the FIRST step is to scrutinise the model, not to build: write the card with Peyton's equations as printed (compartments, the ventilation-perfusion distribution, how inspired and expired alveolar ventilation are related and which one the distribution is defined on, the mass balance for each gas, how uptake changes the expired volume), check that they conserve each gas and reduce to the one-compartment lung when the scatter is zero, and report to Shafer whether the mathematics checks out. Only if it does is a two-region lung (a high and a low ventilation-perfusion region) built into advanceClosedFormGas() and gasArterial(), with its own decision on the scatter's size.
